claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the ability to form a continuous, adherent, thermodynamically stable oxide scale.
Cr2O3 or Al2O3 can serve as the protective oxide scale in these alloys.
A continuous protective oxide scale impedes oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Sufficient concentrations of chromium and/or aluminum promote formation of a protective oxide scale.
Formation of a protective scale leads to lower oxidation rates than in otherwise similar alloys with lower passivating-element concentrations.
Formation of a protective scale improves or preserves material integrity.
Oxide-scale microstructure and continuity mediate oxygen transport into the alloy.
Adequate passivating-element concentrations cause preferential formation of a stable oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
The stable oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion.
Reduced oxygen diffusion lowers the oxidation rate and minimizes internal degradation.
Insufficient passivating-element concentrations produce discontinuous or less adherent oxides.
Discontinuous or poorly adherent oxides cause faster oxidation and loss of material integrity.
Alloys above the passivating-element threshold will have thinner and more continuous oxide layers than the lower-concentration baseline.
Alloys above the passivating-element threshold will show lower oxidation-associated weight change than the baseline.
The proposed governing behavior should hold at temperatures up to about 1200°C when the compared microstructures remain otherwise comparable.
Highly reducing atmospheres or exposure durations that cause phase changes may produce behavior outside the proposed relationship.
